extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and other creative writers interested in using footnotes as a storytelling device
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical guidelines for using footnotes (and similar marginal/end-note devices) as a storytelling technique — either to add worldbuilding/flavor or to tell a secondary/contradictory story. Covers placement, pacing, audio considerations, and framing choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnotes as worldbuilding or flavor
rubrics_metrics.description: Use footnotes to add little tidbits of extra information about setting, history, or characters — the kind of material that doesn’t fit in the main text or might be too much for some readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Footnotes can enrich the world and provide texture without overloading the main narrative. Example: Jonathan Strange and Mr. Norrell’s copious footnotes that expand the magic system. Best when the material genuinely expands the sense of a larger world rather than repeating things already clear in the body text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnotes as a secondary story or twist
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure the work so the main body is a frame and the real story (or a contradictory/secret story) is told in the footnotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The footnotes can reveal secrets, contradictions, or a different perspective that changes how the main text is read. Example: a surface story in the body with a buried, truer story in the notes. This can create a story-within-a-story effect and deliver strong twists if executed clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a reason or frame for footnotes
rubrics_metrics.description: If the footnotes are important, give readers a clear reason to read them (editorial conceit, found-manuscript frame, in-world annotations, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A frame legitimizes footnotes and makes readers more likely to engage with them — e.g., pretending the text is an edited historical manuscript, or that annotations are from an in-world editor. Examples: Princess Bride-style annotations, Jane Austen-mystery conceit. If notes are central, the frame helps them 'belong'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure the story survives without every footnote / plan for optional readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that some readers will skip footnotes; decide whether the main story must still make sense without them or whether you want to pressure readers to read the notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If footnotes are optional flavor, the body should remain coherent when they’re ignored. If notes are essential, use framing or other signals to encourage reading them. Treat some notes as asides if you accept that many will skip them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider audiobook and narration constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes are tied to the physical form of the book and can cause problems in audio formats; you must decide how to handle notes for audiobook production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include skipping unimportant notes, reading them as brief asides, recording them at the end as endnotes (but this loses timing), or using a different narrator/voice for notes. Talk with the narrator about pacing and how to deliver pauses. Remember a large portion of sales may be audio (~40%+), so plan accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnotes affect pacing and rhythm; place markers intentionally
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnote markers force the reader to jump down and back up the page, breaking flow and creating pauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the footnote number where a natural pause exists (e.g., end of a clause/sentence) so readers don’t miss it and have to backtrack. Poor placement leads to disrupted reading and confusion; good placement can create desirable rhythmic beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make footnotes substantive when you expect attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes work best when they themselves read like a story or provide meaningful content rather than throwaway jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the notes are the main attraction (the reader reads for the notes), make them story-like and compelling. Howard’s Planet Mercenary example: in-world document comments that form a 1200-word short story embedded in the book. If notes are just enrichment, lighter treatment is acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use voice and fourth-wall techniques in footnotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes offer an opportunity to address the reader directly, break the narrative fourth wall, or deliver asides in a distinct voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depending on who 'writes' the footnotes (narrator, editor, character), they can create intimacy or commentary. This can increase reader engagement but also changes how the voice is perceived; be deliberate about who is speaking in the notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan narrator strategy for audio (different voices or single narrator)
rubrics_metrics.description: If producing audio, decide whether the footnotes will be read by the same narrator, a different narrator, or omitted, and prepare the reading rhythm accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different narrator voices can make footnotes feel intimate and distinct, but require building different pauses into the performance. If the narrator will not read notes, do not write text that relies on them being heard. Coordinate with actors early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept the trade-off between optional humor and reader attention
rubrics_metrics.description: If footnotes are primarily for jokes or light enrichment (e.g., Squirrel Girl), they can be delightful for some readers but will be missed by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use jokes in notes if you’re comfortable that not all readers will see them. If the joke materially changes understanding, move it into the main text or provide a stronger signal to read the note.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use footnotes for important commentary, context, or references
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes can carry authorial commentary, cultural-context notes, disclaimers, or pointers to further resources when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing sensitive cultural material or providing sources, a footnote can acknowledge choices, direct readers to appendices or external sources, or express editorial intent. Example: Xtreme Dungeon Mastery including a footnote on kishotenketsu and cultural appropriation directing readers to further reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical/format considerations (endnotes vs footnotes; tagging)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to use footnotes (inline bottom-of-page), endnotes, or other marginal devices, and consider the technical implications for digital and audio formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endnotes can be used as a workaround for audio but lose immediacy; tagging notes in digital audio to allow jumps is a possible solution but may be technically complex. Think about the reading/listening experience on different platforms before committing to a format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise: practice adding footnotes to a short story
rubrics_metrics.description: Homework: read 'Stet' by Sarah Gailey and then take a short story you like (or one you wrote) and try adding footnotes that expand the story or reveal a twist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practical exercise encourages testing both uses of footnotes — expansion/worldbuilding and buried-twist — to learn how notes change reader perception and pacing.
